Sir GEORGE FOSTER moved the second reading of Bill No. 82, to provide for the time in Canada being in advance of the solar mean time during the summer months.
He said: It may he advisable that I
should make a short statement with reference to this Bill. Daylight saving is a somewhat new thing in most countries of the world, and ab solutely new, on a national scale, in Canada. The argument? in favour of daylight saving during the summer months are based \ipon a good many considerations. The primary consideration is that of economy. The substitution of an hour of early daylight, which may be used instead of an hour of artificial light, naturally lends itself towards economy, particularly in the matter of lighting, and in the use of coal for the manufacture of gas, and of	electric	light. Outside of these reasons of an economic kind, there are many collateral considerations, which, though not financial, are perhaps more important. The history of daylight saving legislation does not go very far back. I think in 1908 the first Daylight Saving Bill was introduced in the British Parliament, and was referred to a select committee of the House of Commons, which reported in favour of the Bill. It was, however, not enacted. In 1909, another Bill was introduced in the British House of Commons a little wider in scope, and it was also referred to a select committee, which committee reported thereon. Afterwards Bills, were introduced in other sessions, but no legislation followed until 1916, when a resolution introduced by Mr. Henry Norton in favour of legislation along the line of daylight saving in the summer months was carried by a vote of 170 to 2, and in April, 1916, a Bill was passed, which came into operation on the 21st May, and remained in operation until 30th September. It was tested, therefore, in actual operation during 1916. In the -same year legislation for the same purpose was introduced in Germany, Austria, France, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Holland, Portugal, Italy, and perhaps some other smaller countries. In at least ten of the more important European countries daylight saving legislation was adopted in 1916, and was carried into operation. A committee of the House of Commons in Great Britain was appointed to make an examination into the results of the operation of the Daylight Saving Bill, and also to extend their examination and observation, as far as they could, to the other countries in which the system had been in operation. This: committee, after due investigation, has reported, and I shall call the attention of the House to the report. The members of the Hou6e who desire to look into the report more fully will find it in the library.

The first thing to note is the thorough way in which the inquiry was carried out. The committee, in the first place, issued what are now called, -by a modern term, questionnaires, and these were sent to the principal bodies, associations and interests in Great Britain, and to Government institutions, munition factories, industrial concerns, commercial bodies, chambers of commerce, boards of trade, labour unions and organizations, women's unions, co-op-perative societies, in fact they were sent to every particular interest that could be reached in the United Kingdom. Seventy-five per cent of the questionnaires sent out were answered, which is a very large percentage, and shows the interest taken in the matter in Great Britain. The committee gives the comments by the different interests, and the replies from the different interests, and arrive at general conclusions. I shall read a few of the special notes made with reference to special industries, or special interests, and then give the House, in short, the general conclusions that were reached by the committee. As regards public health, in section 19 of the report they say:
We have devoted particular attention to the question of the effects of summer time on the health of children and we have been glad to find that, in spite of certain statements whioh have been made to the contrary, the bulk of the evidence (mostly derived from educational authorities) favours the conclusion that in the case of children summer time has proved a success.
With regard to public morals and order, the committee remarks:
The tendency throughout the country to spend the extra hour of daylight in the evenings out of doors is said of itself to have made for an improvement in the general moral tone. In particular, a marked decrease was noted in some districts in juvenile offences, which is attributed by the police to the fact that during the summer time period boys were expected to be home in daylight.
In reference to the workers' interests generally, it is noted:
So far as the trade unions were concerned, we were not able to obtain quite as much detailed information as we could have wished. However, out of the fourteen trade unions to whom we addressed our circular, we had a definite expression of opinion from nine, the general verdict being favourable in each case, , though one or two of the secretaries remarked that they had not been able to make detailed or extensive inquiry among their members.
In section 25 they say:
The general view of employers as expressed in the replies to the questionnaires was that their employees had taken full advantage of the extra hour's daylight; and while the majority were not in a position, with so short a
fSir George Poster.]
period for observation, to state positively whether or not an improvement in health had resulted, a number had noticed increased vitality in their workers, and in some cases an improvement in the standard of the work. Only one or two employers recorded the appearance of any ill effects in the shape of tiredness and irregularity of time-keeping.
In the opinion of Mr. J. E. 'Hutton, manager of the labour department of Vickers Limited, the Summer Time Act was one of the greatest boons conferred upon the industrial classes of the greater towns and cities by recent legislation. The committee say:
We have had evidence from all sources of the value of the extra daylight to the very large number of workers who cultivate gardens and allotments.
In section 31 they say:
Taking the whole of our evidence, we are satisfied that the great bulk of the working classes are favourable to Summer Time, and we are convinced they stand to profit by it as much as, and in many cases more than, any other section Of the community. Such real inconveniences as have been experienced will, we believe, be remedied with a little more experience of Summer Time conditions.
The committee had the following to say with regard to children's sleep:
Only a very few authorities appear to consider that the evil was so pronounced as to outweigh the other advantages which children derived from the Act. The opinion of a very large majority, and the enthusiastic opinion of a great number, Is that the children benfited by the operation of Summer Time, both by reason of the extra time which they were able to spend in the open air, and also because of the cool hour gained in the morning in place of a trying hour in school in the heat of the afternoon. Many authorities reported that children had been brighter and fresher in the mornings in consequence. This view was confirmed by the medical opinion which we received, and it was unanimously supported by the witnesses who gave evidence before us.
With .regard to trade, industry and commerce, outside of agriculture, the committee notes, in section 37:
The replies received to the very comprehensive inquiries wThich we have described in paragraph 9 above show beyond all question that the opinion of employers in every trade and industry and business throughout the country is overwhelmingly in favour of Summer Time. We summarize the evidence on points of detail, such as effect on the health of workers, saving in artificial light, etc., under the appropriate headings elsewhere in our report.
After showing that there were some diversities of opinion, based upon difficulty in coming to accurate conclusions, in section 42 the committee, dealing with the question of economics in artificial light and fuel, state:

Nevertheless, though it has proved so difficult to arrive at any accurate estimate of the economies effected in light and fuel it is perfectly clear that the substitution of an hour's daylight In the evening during many weeks of the year for an hour's artificial light must have resulted in a considerable net saving; and this is certainly borne out by the information furnished to us. The estimates of the reduction in the consumption of electric light vary very widely, from 1.25 per cent in one case to 55 per cent in another. The returns from the power companies give a mean reduction of 2.0 per cent for lighting purposes. Thirty-eight private companies furnished figures which give an estimate of reduction varying from 10 to 41 per cent, the mean for the thirty-eight being 23 per cent. Sixty-four municipal undertakings give a mean reduction of 18.3 per cent in units used for lighting.
With regard to gas, Mr. Hanbury Thomas, of the Sheffield United Gas Company states:
The total quantity of fuel used by all gas undertakings in the United Kingdom for 1915 was, in round figures, 18,000,000 tons. Reckoning one and one-quarter per cent of these figures, the saving in coal effected by gas undertakings in the United Kingdom as a result of four and a half months of Summer Time may be put at about 260,000 tons.
That was with reference to the saving in coal for the making of gas. The saving to users of gas was estimated at £475,000. The statement is made that 11,500 tons of illuminating oils were saved toy the application of the Daylight Saving Bill.
When you come to agriculture, you have greater diversity of opinion. In section 53 the committee state:
As might have been expected, the opinions of the farmers and those interested in agriculture have been more conflicting than those of any other interest, in many cases totally diverse opinions as to the effect of Summer Time having come from the same district.
We find that the general opinion is that difficulties were easily overcome by organization and that the very definite advantage of having an extra evening hour for carrying crops outweighs any inconvenience. Many reports also mentioned the advantage at harvest time of the help of workers employed in other occupations whose longer evenings made it possible for them to give assistance on the farms. This, of course, occurred chiefly in districts near villages or towns.
Section 55 says:
In some cases trouble was experienced with milkers who were, it is said, unwilling to commence work in the very early mornings, and it is also stated in a few instances that at the outset the quality and quantity of the milk was affected by the earlier milking. These difficulties are only mentioned in a few of the replies, and the majority even of these few add that they were only temporary.
The committee say in section 56:
In the gathering and transit of fruits and vegetables the operation of the Act is generally reported to have been very beneficial, as in almost all cases these are better gathered with the dew on and transported during the cool of the day.
Section 59 says:
In spite of 'such difficulties as have been recorded, a very large majority of farmers and war agricultural committees are in favour of a renewal of the Act, and the majority even of those who are of opinion that it was not advantageous to agriculture consider that it should be renewed, as they recognize its great benefits to the community at large.
In respect to the later closing of shops, the evidence is stated to have been almost overwhelmingly in favour of the Daylight Saying Act.	_
These take in the main points in the special observations of the committee with reference to the results of their examination,
I will n<5w read the three concluding paragraphs entitled " conclusions " of their report which are general:
Taking the evidence we have received as a whole, we can unhesitatingly say that the vast preponderance of opinion throughout Great Britain is enthusiastically in favour of Summer Time and of its renewal-not only as a war measure, but as a permanent institution.
As we have already pointed out, some difficulties have undoubtedly been experienced, but not to anything like the extent predicted by the critics of the scheme, and we have not heard of any that could not be overcome with goodwill and organization. Indeed the experience of Summer Time in 1916 has converted many of its former opponents into hearty supporters. Moreover, as we have pointed out elsewhere, many of those who still hold the view that Summer Time may be prejudicial to their own interests admit that the general public advantages arising from it more than outweigh any inconveniences that may be caused in particular cases. In a few years we believe that what opposition still remains to Summer Time will have completely disappeared, and that the whole nation will regard it as a wholly beneficent measure.
We recommend, therefore, that Summer Time should be re-introduced in 1917 and in subsequent years.
As a result of that report the Summer Time Bill was again introduced and was passed with practical unanimity, and it is for the second year in operation in the United Kingdom. Similar investigations were undertaken to get at the results of the operation of the measure in France in 1916, and the report has been so far satisfactory that in France again the Daylight Saving Bill has become law for the present year and is in operation. Daylight saving measures are also in operation for the second year in the northern fringe of neutral countries that I have mentioned, and in Italy, and a similar measure has been introduced and passed for the first time in Australia.

It will be noted that after the introduction and trial of a daylight saving measure, almost all of these countries have, after investigation, been so far influenced by the operation during the preceding year that they have put it into operation for the second year, and the report of the British committee recommended that the Daylight Saving Bill not only be passed for the year 1917, but that it be passed for successive years. The matter has been taken up in the United States, and an extended hearing commencing, I think, in March, was given by a Senate committee. Before that committee, opinions were brought from every part of the United States. The hearing has been concluded, and as a result the United States Senate has passed a Daylight Saving Bill by a large majority and has sent it to the House of Representatives, where it is believed that the Bill will pass with an equally strong majority. Inasmuch, however, as a large part of the summer season has been taken up, in the United States, in holding the hearings and passing the Bill through the Senate and .as the Bill, with other pressing legislation, has to pass through the House of Representatives, it is provided that the measure shall go into operation not this year but at the designated period in 1918.
In Canada we have had various experiments made with daylight saving, but in restricted areas, and, ef course, it is quite easily seen that when such a measure is put into force in a city or a small district, while surrounding cities and the generality of the country are not under the operation of a similar Act, it does not have its full force and effect. Even so, there are strong testimonies in favour of the good effect of daylight saving in various cities and towns in which it was in operation last year. The general impression, however, so far as far as I have gathered, is that it is shorn of its main and proper advantages unless it becomes ian extended measure-unless, in fact, it becomes a national measure. Some opinions are expressed that it would be better if, when a daylight saving measure goes into operation, it should go into operation contemporaneously with the Act in the United States, so that, along the border line where we have our traffic arrangements, there should be no clash of time keeping as between the two countries. As part of the summer is now past, and holding in view the suggestion that I mentioned last, I think it is reasonable to say that if this Bill is passed, a provision should

be inserted in it bringing it into effect next year when, in all probability, it will have the 'added support of similar legislation in the United States. As regards the demand for a daylight saving measure in Canada, there is a wide call for it from every part of the Dominion. There are also objections against it.
Sir WILFRID LAURilER:	What are
they?

The call for legislation is generally from the manufacturing industries, the 'boards of trade and business associations of the towns and cities. The objections to the legislation that have so far come to hand are from sections of the farming community who foresee trouble iin certain lines of their work in the earlier time to be set, and inconveniences that would arise therefrom. It is fair to say that those are in restricted lines. of agriculture. What I. have read from the British committee's report would show that the same objections were held there; when the legislation was first introduced, but that upon the whole the agricultural interests, in Britain, being aware that the general advantages were entirely in favour of the legislation, are by a large majority in favour of the reenactment of the daylight saving law. The House will note that I have not put forward any particular plea either for or against such legislation in this country. What I was anxious to do was to place before the House a brief summary of what had been done and why it had been done so that members, if they had not been able to follow the outcome of similar legislation in other countries, might have the advantage of knowing what the result had been.
Personally, I am very strongly in favour of such legislation, largely on the ground of economy, but still more largely on the ground of public health and morals and the maintenance of social order, which seem to spring from the substitution of an hour of daylight for an hour of artificial light. Stress is laid in the British report upon the impetus given to production by the cultivation of small garden plots. These plots, though small in themselves, when cultivated all over the country, contribute tremendously to the food production of the nation. In that respect the British report is entirely favourable to daylight saving.
With this statement, I leave the matter before the House. I shall be glad of a discussion, if that is deemed wise, and we can then go into committee on the Bill,

and leave it there until the House has had an opportunity of digesting the information and coming to a conclusion.

As this Bill
seems to be very technical and more information will he' required, I would suggest that the discussion had better take place in committee rather than upon the second reading.	-

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Blain in the Chair.
On section 2-time advanced one hour:

What is the prescribed
period in the United States?

It runs from
somewhere in April to the latter part of September or about the 1st of October.

The object of the Bill, in a nutshell, is that we shall, by law, call what is .seven O'clock, eight o'clock, and what is eight o'clock, nine o'clock. I agree that the object is a very praiseworthy one, but whether it is necessary to achieve the object by legislation is quite another matter. It is true that most of the civilized countries of Europe furnish us with precedents at the present time. Legislation, of this sort is an attempt to make us believe that a certain hour is really a different hour. The labourer's day generally commences at seven o'clock, at which hour all the factory whistles are heard summoning the labourers to their day's work. The school boy's day begins at nine, and the business man goes to his office about ten o'clock. Now, this Bill proposes that the labourer shall begin his day's work at six o'clock instead of seven, the school boy at eight o'clock instead of nine, and the business man at nine o'clock instead of ten. It i'S quite possible for these three classes to being their day's work one hour earlier without any legislation on the subject .at .all, and I think it would be we.ll if they agreed to do so voluntarily. If the captains of .industry would start their men working at six instead of seven o'clock in the summer time, and .the schools would o.pen at eight and the business offices at nine, the same object would be achieved. But it has been thought that confusion would .arise without the authority of the law upon the subject. I agree with my hon. friend that the report he has read justifies his conclusions. Without deceiving ourselves in this w.ay, I think it would he to our advantage if we all rose .an hour earlier
in the .summer time. But when we have the force of law behind us we shall have to be industrious whether we will or no, and when five o'clock in the morning comes, though we know it is only five o'clock, the Bill says it is six o'clock and we shall have to get up. So far, so good; I have no objection.
There is one point, however, that does no:t seem to have been considered. In Europe the area of the different countries is very limited. In England, for instance, a few hours' ride brings, you to the end of the Kingdom. In France, you can leave Baris at iany time of the day land reach the frontier before the following morning. But it is different on this continent. It takes over four clays to get from Halifax to Vancouver, and the same length of time to get from New York to the Pacific Ocean. Now the railways have a .standard time of their own, which varies .according to latitude. Has my hon. friend considered how railway time will he affected by this Bill? If this Bill is .passed and comes into operation next year, when it is ten o'clock by solar time it will be eleven o'clock under this Bill. In the city of Ottawa to-day, I think we are using railway time and not solar time.
Standard time.

That is railway time. My hon. friend would perhaps explain whether there would he any conflict with railway time. For my part I see no objection to the Bill; it ought to work well. But I think it would be better for the health of every one of us, and (to out .advantage in the other respects to which my bon. friend has referred, if of our own free will we rose an hour earlier in the summer time.

As to the area of the different countries, the United States is within a few square miles as large as Canada, and no difficulty has been encountered there. A very thorough inquiry was first of all made, at which the railway companies were represented. That is a fact which in itself .serves for any amount of other evidence that I oonld give. Then with reference to the railways, I will read the opinion of Sir George Bury, vice-president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which I think would be taken as good testimony so far as the railway part of it is concerned.
There may he various views on the advisability of daylight saving, but there is one point on which there is no diversity of opinion, and that is that if daylight saving is to be successful it must be a measure passed by the Government at Ottawa, which would require that all

clocks in the Dominion be set ahead one hour ..at a stated time in the early spring, and set back an hour at a stated time in the fall.
The daylight saving scheme has been tried in many localities, and the main reason for its failure was entirely due to it not having been universally adopted all over Canada.
As I see it, if the people of Canada as a whole wish daylight saving, it tehould be adopted ; and so far as the railways are concerned, I believe they would gladly support it. If it were made universal in Canada, it could not, in any way, embarrass train operation.

I can quite understand that so far as the railways are concerned it plays no part whatever, because for some years past we have been com-
5 p.m. pelled to adopt railway time in Canada. We know railway time is not solar time, but simply a conventional time. The earth is divided into sections, starting at Greenwich, every fifteen degrees east or west represents an hour in time. When they get back fifteen degrees, they drop an hour. Thirty degrees means two hours. Forty-five degrees means three hours, and sixty degrees four hours. That brings you to what we call Atlantic Standard time. I think the first degree would be somewhere around Cape Breton island, therefore, under present conditions, the people of Cape Breton island are practically solar time. Wherever you come to the centre of one of those sections, you have practically solar time. As you go east from the centre their time is slower than solar time, and as you go west it is faster than solar time. To my mind that is the whole difficulty in Canada. Although it does not make any difference to the railways, it makes a great deal of difference to the people. I happen to live on the very western edge of the Atlantic Standard time, and our time is half an hour faster than solar time. When you cross the boundary line into the state of Maine you are under the eastern standard time, which, I think has its centre very near Montreal, and which brings Montreal practically under solar time. As you go east they are slower until you get to the eastern border of the state of Maine or the western border of New Brunswick, where they are half an hour slower than eastern standard time. Going west, when you reach North Bay or Sudbury you come to the western edge of the eastern standard time, and there they are half an hour faster. I understand the railway company takes Fort' William as the dividing point between the two times, but that is only conventional, because they are taking much more than the fifteen degrees into the eastern standard time, and I think you will find the next section has much less 
than fifteen degrees. I just mention this to impress upon the minister the fact that in a country extending as far east and west as Canada does you have great inequalities now. It would perhaps be feasible to advance the clock an hour if you are at the centre of one of these sections, but, when you get west of the centre, where the time is faster than it ought to be, arid you advance it another hour, you are getting people out of bed in the night in order that they may be up at six or seven o'clock in the morning. They tried this daylight saving in St. John last year, and it was a great failure. The difficulty was that their time is about twenty-five minutes fast.
Twenty-four minutes.	[DOT]

I think I made a pretty good estimate of it. St. John standard time i.s 24 or 25 minutes faster than St. John solar time. Then they added an hour on to that, and there was great confusion, because the Canadian Pacific Railway carries its eastern standard time down to St. John, which is nearly 100 miles east of the eastern limit of the eastern standard section. The result is they had three times in St. John, the Canadian Pacific Railway time, Atlantic Standard time (which is legal time in New Brunswick) and this daylight saving time. I know that country pretty well, yet I had a great deal of difficulty in getting out of St. John one Sunday.	.
They do not travel on Sunday down there.

Yes, they do occasionally. I could hardly tell what time the train left, so I simply went to the station and waited for it. If you compel the railway companies to adopt this daylight saving time, you will probably bring about a great deal of confusion. In this world there are a great many faddists as regards everything. Perhaps they are useful in some ways, but it has always appeared to me that this was one of the greatest fads ever put before the public. If you are going to adopt this Daylight Saving Bill, it. can only be in effect during the summer months, when we have a great deal more sunlight than we know what to do with. If you were at the Tropic of Cancer, within a few degrees of the Equator, I can see it might make some difference, because the farther north you go the greater the variations in the length of the days and of the nights, until you get to the Arctic Circle, and from there to the North Pole, theoretic-

ally you have a point where there are six months days and six months nights. In Canada on the 21st of June we have daylight from four o'clock in the morning until half-past eight in the evening, and as you go backward, or go forward, from the 20th of March until the 21st of September, when you have the equinoxes, you have more or less daylight. People in this country usually start to work at seven o'clock in the morning, and under this scheme you practically put them to work at six o'clock, solar time. But you have daylight for two hours before that. There is no saving of oil, light, coal, or .power. On the other hand, they cease work at six o'clock and there are two hours of daylight after that.
Three.

There would be under this scheme if they ceased work at five o'clock solar time. That would give three and a half hours after the day's work was done. There is, I repeat, no saving of power, light, coal or oil in manufacturing establishments. It would not mean anything in the stores, because in the summer time the stores all over the country close in the evening. In our province we have a compulsory law on the subject. If two or three storekeepers petition the Government, they issue an order compelling all storekeepers to close at six o'clock. Therefore, there is no saving as far as the stores are concerned. It simply comes down to the question of a little bit of saving in the homes of the people. We all know that people will not go to bed in the summer time until it gets dark. You can make all the laws that all the faddists in the United States or Canada ask you to make, but they will not have any effect. The Anglo-Saxon says: It is my business when I go to bed, and I am not going to bed until after dark. The country will bum just as much oil and coal as it did formerly. While in many cases this system may be an advantage, while east of the centre line of these different sections or standards it would be an advantage, it would be such a great disadvantage to those people living west of the centre line that I am afraid the disadvantage would far outweigh the advantage. I believe that wherever it has been ' tried in Canada it has not been a success. However, if the minister is anxious to have it go through I am not going to vote against it, but it is only pursuing one of those pleasant discussions which are matters of entertainment but have no practical value.

This notice has been on the Order Paper so long that I was in hopes that it would stay there until the session closed. I agree entirely with the remarks of the last speaker. If you have more daylight than you know what to do with in the East, we certainly have in the West. You say that you have daylight at four o'clock in the East and that it is dark at eight. In the West you have daylight at half-past two and you can see to read at ten o'clock.
You are that much farther north.
Yes, and west.
Being west has nothing to do with it; it is a matter of'north and south.

The report read by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce applies to England and possibly the continent of Europe. The conditions are not parallel as between Great Britain and Canada. You may say that the United States would perhaps present a parallel case. Did I understand the minister to say that a daylight saving law had been adopted there?
It has passed the Senate.

We tried this out locally in Winnipeg and Brandon last year. Brandon stood it for one month, but as it was more difficult to abolish it at Winnipeg it lasted during the summer. When the council was called upon this spring to express itself with regard to daylight saving, it unanimously decided to go back to the old, tried and reliable time which has stood us in good stead for a great many centuries and is good enough for us now. People will not go to bed, even although the clock shows 11 o'clock. They will say: It is not eleven o'clock, it is only ten o'clock and are going to stay up another hour. In my opinion the farmers of western Canada are almost a unit against the adoption of this Bill and in favour of the system that we have at present. Coming from the West, where we have a tremendous amount of daylight, it occurs to me-and I say this without the slightest desire to be offensive -that, with a temperature of 81 degrees of this House and the session nearing the first of August, we might be occupying our time better with some other measures than talking about saving'daylight.

The hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) says that he has requests from various boards of trades and cities throughout the country in favour of this Daylight Saving Bill. I did not catch what he said about agriculture, 'but I do not know of any agriculturists who want the time set forward an hour. What good would it be to them? They get up at daylight and they work until dark. They put in fourteen or fifteen hours a day. What is going to be saved by fixing the time earlier? They would have to get up and milk the cows, as my hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean) says, at three o'clock in the morning. The cows will object if they are disturbed an hour earlier. Then, what about the roosters-are they going to start to crow an hour earlier?

In reference to
the roosters, they get in enough work now.

That is what I say too. They waken us up, heaven knows, early enough now without starting them an hour, earlier. I cannot understand, in so far as the agricultural community is concerned, where there will be any benefit. They have to get up at five; milking starts at half past five, and they work until seven in the evening. There would not be any benefit at all in getting them up at four instead of five. Then, in the evening they will not go to bed, as my hon. friend from Carle-ton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) has said, until after dark. They do not go to bed in daylight even on the farm. Therefore I do not see any benefit that can accrue on the farm. As to the manufacturer, he starts at seven o'clock and closes at six. It is daylight long before he starts, and he is not required to use artificial light except on a dark day, unless his shop is badly lighted.
I do not suppose that moving the clo.ck forward an hour will affect the darkness of a shop of that kind. If he works in a dark shop he will have to put on artificial lights but if he has a light shop he will not need any light. The hours of work will be the same. As far .as fuel is concerned, if he works eight or ten hours, he will use just the same amount of fuel whether he works in daylight or darkness. Therefore I do not see any possibility of saving in fuel. I can easily understand boards of trade asking for this because they largely consist of lawyers, doctors and merchants who like to close up early and go for a game of golf. But that will not help the country one bit. There is lots of time after

closing at six o'clock for golf, tennis or bowling. I do not -see any benefit in this thing, and I do not know where my hon. friend gets his petitions from. I cannot imagine what business or class it will benefit, except the gentlemen whom I have mentioned. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean), I have no doubt, would like a law passed so that he would not have to get up at all, but I do not believe it will help the rest of us any.

If the farmers are forced to get up an hour earlier, I do not think the cows would give nearly so much. The farmers are wakened up when they should be sleeping. I think changing the time twice a year would be a great inconvenience. Hon. members fail to realize what it means for the farmers to get up at half past four or five. The farmers cannot get to work, from haying till harvest is over, till almost eight o'clock. They cannot work while the dew is on the ground. If the time is put back, it is going to injure the farmers. The men working on the farms will see that the men in villages stop work at five o'clock in the afternoon, and they will want to do the same. Some of the people in the county I represent want the time changed, but only a small percentage. I am sure that not one farmer in my county desires to see the change, and I think it would be a great mistake.

There is one argument
which has not, so far, been advanced in this discussion. I heard a good deal of complaint in the West about the daylight saving scheme. It came chiefly from two classes of people, the farmers throughout the country and the women in the cities. In the case of the farmer, the chief objection was that farmers living ten, twelve or fifteen miles from a town, after they got through their day's work, would run into town in their automobiles, but would find that the stores -were closed an hour earlier than previously. The daylight saving did not affect the farmers themselves, because they got up just as early as before the time was changed, but it would shut them off from the opportunity of doing business in the stores in the villages and small towns.
I heard a great many complaints in Winnipeg from the women. Their complaint was that the children got up an hour earlier, and they simply could not get them to bed any earlier at night, because, as everybody knows, in Winnipeg, for several months in the summer, it is daylight until

ten o'clock at night. There was very, very great complaint about the change. There may 'be some advantages in it that we have not heard of, but take it all round, I do not think there is any great demand in Canada for daylight saving.

I do not think public opinion generally is behind this movement, and I will waste only a few moments in discussing it. Last year, in the city of London they tried an experiment in this matter, the movement 'being agitated, I think, by the Board of Trade, or by petition from a number of merchants. The plan was found to work very unsatisfactorily. It dislocated business and disorganized things generally, and it was only allowed to remain in operation for about a month, when opposition to it developed so strongly that the city council saw it was a mistake and cancelled the by-law. I find a great deal of opposition to it amongst the farming community in my district. Farmers generally [were inconvenienced, and when, this year, they saw that a movement was inaugurated to promote this scheme I received from different farmers communications expressing decided objection to the proposed Bill. I think business men and farmers generally will be more satisfied if the time remains as it is.

As far as I can see, it
would, be felt more especially in the large cities, particularly in Montreal, where the tramway service is not what it should be. It would be different if we had an underground road to carry the vast hordes of people, who go to work early in the morning and have to cover eight, ten, twelve or fourteen miles before they reach their work. A large number of working people have to leave their homes an hour, or an hour and a half, before the time they are supposed to commence wor|k. It would mean that these people would have to get up very early. We have had a great deal of inconvenience in Bonaventnre. We have the Eastern Standard time, Altantic Standard, and 'the local mean time, so that it brought about a confusion which has not ended yet. As to -a measure of this kind, it will not affect the districts which are remote from the towns, because tbe farmer residing a long distance from tbe city does not need to go to the market with his truck in the morning, and does not care at what hours the stores open or close. As the season is very short, he will get up as early as he can,_ and do all the work he can possibly do, because he
234i
only has three or four months in the year in which he can do any work at all. As far as those who are in (the cities are concernr ed, I tihink the proposition, could not be enforced successfully-for instance, in a place like Montreal-until the method and customs of the people are changed. In Montreal, especially in the summer evenings, .there 'are attractions galore for the young people, moving picture shows and parks of various kinds, and it is very difficult to get them to go to bed early. If these people keep up their present hour's, and are compelled to go to work an hour earlier in the -morning, I think -there will! he such an outcry that the Bill will not work at all.

The right hon. gentleman- (Sir George Foster) read some reports wiith regard to the experience in the working of this law in England, and, amongst other things, said that the -application of -this law had resulted in- a great saving in expense for fuel and light. I cannot understand that. Cam the hon. gentleman explain, it? What difference would it make in the cost of -fuel to -anybody. There is no saving of fuel as far as I oan -see, or [DOT] of -light either, because in either case, the working hours in summer are all in daylight. It may be different in England, but -as far as thi-s country is concerned, I cannot see the force of his observation.

The conditions
are different in England from the conditions here, because their evenings are not -so long. The facts as brought out by the examination are stated, and I have no doubt of those facts. Here, where we have such 1-ong hours- of daylight, similar -saving will not take place in the items of electric light land gas, although I think there would be fairly good economy, even in respectt of those two items, particularly as regards home consumption.
I have no disposition to force the Bill upon the House, if the House does not care to endorse it. I felt it my duty, in answer to very widespread requests-and a-s this legislation would be in consonance with that enacted in other great countries of the world-to introduce the Bill. I h-ave presented it, and I have frankly made a statement of the case before the House. I propose now to leave it in committee, and we cam- use onr judgment with reference to the future progress of the measure.

Before the hon. gentleman takes any further action, I would point out one difference -between 'Canada and the United States, as far as daylight saving i-s

-concerned. In Canada; as pointed out by horn. gentlemen from the West, we have more daylight than we know what to do with in'the summer time, but my horn. , friend is sufficient of an astronomer to know that the further north yon go the longer the days in -summer time and the -shorter in winter. If my hon. friend would go down to the southern portion of the United States, say Texas, I do not imagine it, would be daylight before five o'clock in the morning, and it would be dark at seven in the evening on the 21et of June. Conditions are different here from what they are in the United States, because we are farther north. The southern part of New Brunswick is in latitude 45 or 46. In our part of the country in June it gets dark at about half past eight. In Winnipeg and in the country north of that city, where the latitude is about 50 degress, it does not get dark until ten o'clock. I can understand that in Massachusetts, Pennsylvania -and the southern part of New York state, the people might well take advantage of an extra hour in the morning, because they have not as m-uoh daylight to s-pare as we have. In Canada, nothing is gained by changing the time. You only disarrange the affairs of the people, and you do not make the saving that would he made by the adoption of such a measure in the central portion of the United States.

I think that the people of the part of the country from which I come would be in favour of this Bill. For some years we have had what is called "fast time" in Regina-it is by the working out of these things that we determine whether or not they are beneficial. In spite of the fact that in Regina the change of time involves all the inconveniences of having time which is different from the railway time and from the time in the neighbouring towns, year after year they have resorted to fast time during the summer. That is our practical experience.
Is the Regina time faster or slower than the standard time?

The Regina time would be -pTetty nearly the same as the solar time. Regina is less than one hundred miles from the point where the Canadian Pacifio train-men change the time of their watches. I cannot answer -my -hon. friend's question in any more detail. There is, however, that specific illustration in the case of Regina. Then there is this point:	at

all those places where the people have the option of taking whichever -time they, want, the people invariably go by the fast ti-sie. It is evident, therefore, that in its practical working out there is some convenience in the adoption of the faster time. It is a fact that we waste a great deal of daylight in- the morning -and that the average citizen is out o-f bed a great deal of the time after sunset. If you can do anything to equalize things by devoting the hours of darknes-s more exclusively to sleep, you are that much ahead in the enjoyment of life, and in the saving of light, and any other way you want to 'look at it. Personally I am very much in, favour of this Bill.
Mr. M-cCRANEY:	A few years ago in
the city of Saskatoon we had a by-law providing for the changing of time. On account of the railways having standard time, there was -a great deal of confusion, and that gave rise to some objection to the daylight saving plan. During the summer, before th-e term of the by-law had run out, the bylaw was cancelled, for the reason given by the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff): the difficulty parents had in getting their children off the streets and getting them to bed. I -do not think that they would ask for it again.

There seems to be a consensus of opinion against this Bill. But, as with most Bills, there are two sides to the question involved. Most of the argument that I have heard this afternoon has been in favour of the agricultural committees; I want to say a word on behalf of the employees of the manufacturers. I think that if a vote were taken among the men employed in the manufacturing concerns of Canada, they would express themselves as largely in favour of this Bill. From my own practical experience, I am satisfied that the change would be a great benefit. Hon. gentleman may be surprised when I tell them that under present conditions the factories sometimes change their working hours in order to suit the hours of light and in order to prevent lighting up both morning and evening. In the spring they change the time one way, say half an hour; and in the fall they change it the other way. But another reason why the majority of men and women employed in the manufacturing industries are in favour of this legislation is that they all look forward to the evening as a time of pleasure. As it is now, by the time these people get home from their work, get cleaned up and do what they have to do about the house, they have not much time for pleasure. A man who has a garden, for

instance, always looks forward to the evening -as the time when he will do necessary work in the garden. I am satisfied that most of these men would rather go to work earlier in the morning and have that extra hour in the evening.
Why not hoe the garden in the morning?

It is all very well to say that, but most of these men find it all they can do to get up in the morning, get their breakfast and get to work in time. If daylight saving were adopted, they would have the advantage of that extra hour in the morning, and they would get to work just as conveniently as they do now. I believe that they would prefer going to work an hour earlier in the morning for the sake of getting the extra hour in the evening.
Progress reported.

This is an
increase of $125,000 over last year. This vote covers all the expenditures for salaries of officers, permanent and temporary; the contingencies of the various offices in both eastern and western divisions; the salaries and contingencies of the Board of Grain Commissioners; and the working expenses of the different Government elevators,
interior and terminal, from Vancouver eastward. The crop of 1913 ^as very much larger than was anticipated; in fact, it wras the largest crop in the history of the country, so that a supplementary vote had to be taken last year to meet the expenses of the year. As between the two years, therefore, the great crop of 1915, which commenced coming out late in the autumn and continued coming out during the year 1916, caused the extra work and consequently the extra expenditure. Generally, after the usual rush of grain at the close of navigation, there is a lull, and so much work does not have to be carried on, but the crop of 1915 came out with very little lull; it was coming out during the whole season, and as soon as the season of navigation opened again in the spring of 1916, the rush was very great.
After the close of navigation it came out by railway?
Yes.
To Montreal?

It came up to the western terminals, and a good deal of it came down to Montreal. Some figures might be enlightening. At Winnipeg and other western points, for the crop year ending 31st August, 1916, 354,039 cars containing over 474,000,000 bushels of grain were inspected. The preceding year the figures were 122,831 cars containing 153,000,000 bushels. That is, in 1915, there were about three times as many cars and about three times as many bushels of grain as in the preceding year-cars from year to year taking a greater number of bushels of grain. In the crop year of 1916, for ten months to June 30, 1917, there -were inspected 212,000 cars containing 279,000,000 bushels of grain, or an excess over the crop year of 1914 of about 89,000 cars and more than 126,000,000 bushels of grain. That accounts for the increased work of the staff.
Does the minister purpose, during this -session, bringing in a Bill to amend the Canada Grain Act?

I have already been questioned three or four times by my hon. friend and have made answer that I thought it would bp necessary. Some of the things that I had at that time in mind I regard now, after investigation, as not of sufficient importance to make it necessary to bring them in, but there are one or two points which I think will have to be dealt' with by legislation, and at the present time

I expect to bring in a very short Bill in amendment of the Act.

I understand ihat $2.40
is the maximum price. If an arrangement is made to take over the whole crop at a certain price for No. 1 Northern at Fort William, the price of flour should also be

fixed; the millers should not be allowed to charge what they like. It takes about 50,000,000 bushels of wheat to furnish the people of Canada with a year's supply of flour. It is well known what it costs to grind a barrel of flour, and what the	handling and	shipping charges
are, and I repeat that the miller should be allowed to charge not more than a certain price. Otherwise the consumer will have to pay for flour at a much higher rate than the farmer is paid for his wheat, and we shall have a repetition of what happened last year when the middlemen got away with millions of dollars that should have been saved to the consumers. Personally, I think it would be a good thing all round if such an arrangement was made. There is only one customer anyway; Britain is buying for herself and her Allies. I was up in the West recently, and the farmers with whom I discussed this question were all willing to accept a reasonable price. I never heard one suggest so high a figure as that mentioned by my hon. friend.

What does my hon.
friend consider a fair and reasonable price?

I represent only farmers; I do not represent consumers in the ordinary sense of the word. In my judgment a reasonable price would be $2 for No. 1 Northern at Fort William, which would give $1.80 to $1.87 a bushel to the ordinary farmer in the Middle West. I think that price would be satisfactory to the farmer, providing he knew the consumers of Ontario and the lower provinces were getting their flour on that basis, instead of having to pay on the basis of $2.50 a bushel. I do not want to be understood as giving this price on behalf of the farmers; I was not deputed by any farmer to state a price, but I think the figure I mentioned would be fair as between the farmers I represent and the consumers that other hon. gentlemen represent.
Is the hon. gentleman desirous of fixing a price for next year's crop or for - this year's crop only?
I was speaking of this year's crop.	.
My hon. friend would not go beyond this year's crop?
No, I had not that in mind.

Now that the bars are all down and wheat can flow freely into the

United States from western Canada, how can the price be regulated at Fort William? If the Americans happen to offer a little more than $2 a bushel, the farmer would certainly not send his wheat to Fort William to be sold at $2.

I understand-and the Minister of Trade and Commerce can correct me if I am wrong-that the Governments of Great Britain, the United States and Canada are negotiating an arrangement for the handling of the crop of both the United States and Ganada. If the Canadian Government or the Wheat Commission made arrangements for buying the whole crop, a fair and reasonable price would be fixed, and everybody would have to live up to the agreement. I think you would find that the great majority of farmers would be satisfied with an arrangement of that kind, though no doubt there will always be some who would not be satisfied with $2 if there was a chance of selling somewhere else for $2.50. I have never heard a farmer express himself as not being satisfied with an arrangement of that kind.
I understood my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) to ask this question with reference to the 1916-17 crops?

I was referring to the growing crop that will be on the market in two or three months. I quite understand that the 1916 crop is in the hands of the people who bought it, and it might be said we were confiscating their property if we made arrangements regarding the 1916 crop.

The discussion covered both crops, I think. I wanted to make sure what my hon. friend's question was. The matter divides itself along certain broad and general lines. First of all there is one buyer, that buyer being the Allies, represented by whatever commission or committee they may set up. There will be a common buyer for the allied demands, and consequently they will not be competing against each other
The seller is divided into two. There is the seller in the United States, and the seller in Canada, and an arrangement will no doubt be made as to the price that shall be paid, having regard to both the buyer, who must have the grain, and the seller who furnishes the supply. The reason blatters have drifted along so far as they have without fixation of price or without such controlling and supervising regulations and methods as will be adopted, is that there is no -United States authority yet established with power to act. In Canada we
have the advantage of a War Measures Act by which Parliament gives the Government powers which are very broad and which cover a matter of this kind absolutely. Such a law does not exist in the United States, consequently the two Houses must legislate for these powers; and for the last six weeks or more they have been coming to conclusions as to just what legislation they should pass, what powers they will give, and what regulations and restrictions they will authorize to be made. Until the United States commission, or whatever it may be called, has its powers defined and is in a position to act, there must necessarily be delay and imperfect co-operation between Canada and the United States on this question. We all agree that, constituted as we are, it is advisable that the two countries should act together in reference to the prices of wheat. Our wheat goes into the United States without let or hindrance, and the market price is there accessible to the seller in Canada. It is expected that this week, or next week at the latest, the legislation will have been perfected, and then the United States authority will be constituted and its powers defined. In Canada, we have placed the matter in the hands of a Board of Supervisors, the constitution of which has been declared. The Order in Council has been laid before Parliament, and the powers of the Board are therein defined. That commission has visited Washington, and has had full communication and conference with the authorities there; and, so far as the crop of 1917-18 is concerned, it is the desire of our commission and of the United States authorities to act together. Just as soon as the legislation is through at Washington, just so soon oan the two bodies take accordant action. I do not think any prices will be set for the crop of 1917-18 until the preliminaries I have mentioned have been discussed.

Will the minister
pardon me for a moment? I have just picked up the afternoon paper, and I find that the gamblers are betting that wheat at Winnipeg will be worth $2.31! in October. They are betting that July wheat will be worth $2.58; I believe that is in the Chicago market-they are betting that September wheat will be worth $2.31. I quite realize the almost insurmountable difficulty in applying the law in Canada and not in the United States, but just as long as the matter is allowed to drift, just so long will the gamblers

continue their betting, and when a man bets a Jew million dollars that wheat will be worth so much, he will move heaven and earth to see that nothing beats him on his bet. He will go to the Government, or will go 'anywhere, and say: I have so much tied up in options on September-or October-or December-wheat, and if you regulate the price at lower than $2.31 I am ruined. I would like to see something done that, if these men go on gambling on the price of wheat and are ruined, they shall have no one but themselves to blame. I think notice should be given to these people by the Government that if they will gamble they do so at their oiwn risk. The time has come when there should be very drastic action taken in Canada, not only in regard to the price of wheat but in regard to the prices of many other commodities. It is absolutely unreasonable that the consuming public should
5 p.m. be compelled to pay the prices they have been paying in many instances. Even if the United States will not pass the legislation, we have the power to prohibit the exportation of wheat from Canada, and we have the power to fix the price. Therefore, so far as Canada is concerned, we can at least protect our own people. Of course, the prohibition of the exportation of wheat is a last resort, and I hope it will not be necessary for us to go that far. At the same time, I feel we should point out to those gamblers that the food of the people must not be put up to unreasonable prices in order that they may satisfy their greed for money which they have not earned.

Of course, we cannot prevent people from betting on what the price of wheat will be in September or October. As I was saying, the matter divides itself into two sections. There is the 1916-17 crop which remains on hand, which I do not think is subject to the limitations that the crop of 1917-18 would be subject to on the ground of accordance between the two countries under the regulations or control which they shall have.t There is not ,a ftarge quantity of the 1916-17 wheat in store in Canada, although there is a considerable quantity of it; a very large proportion of that, I believe-a larger portion than I had thought- is owned actually by farmers, and is held for a price. The advantage of whatever price it is sold at, if it be an advantage, will accrue to the farmers who

are holding the wheat in different storage elevators.
There cannot be very much sympathy with a farmer who refuses to sell his wheat for $3 a bushel.

I suppose the
farmer might not have exactly the same view of it. It is important at the present time that the surplus of wheat in Canada should find its market tand transfer from Canada at the very earliest possible moment. This is rendered necessary for two reasons-in the first place because arrangements have been made for the carriage of wheat up to the quantity of our surplus, and we do not want to retard these transportation arrangements in any way.
It is not impossible-I do not say that it will be done-that the board of Grain Supervisors will fix the price for the 1916-17 crop, which is now in store, independently entirely of what action may be taken in the United States in reference to their 1916-17 crop. The food controller, who has been appointed, takes up the problem where the Board of Grain Supervisors leaves it. They have to do with wheat and grain only. The moment they act upon wheat and grain, the food controller knows whiat the price * of the basic article is and then can conduct his work on a fixed and certain basis, provided the arrangement for price fixation is for the total crop. There will then be no debate and matters will be simple in so far as the basic price of the prime article of food is concerned. I do not think I can say anything more in reference to this matter. The delay is regrettable. The Winnipeg Grain Exchange is not allowing any dealings in futures, and consequently speculation is shut off from the exchange.

What is the meaning of
the announcement of the figure of $2.40 spoken of by my hon. friend from Carleton?

I have heard
nothing oflmially at all about the fixing of the price of the present crop in store. I just saw it in the paper but I have no official knowledge of it. I do not know whether it is true or not true.

The newspapers contained the very definite announcement that the Board of Grain Supervisors had established a figure of $2.40 a bushel for No. 1 Northern at Fort William. I rather understood from my reading of the item that this was the maximum price beyond which the grain of the coming year's crop should not be sold after August 1. Was it merely the

maximum price or was it a price at which it was expected grain would he taken off the farmers' hands?
Mr. CAB,VELL: May I ask my hon. friend a question? Does he think there will be any practical difference between fixing a maximum price and setting the price at $2.40? Would it not be $2.40 any way?
I am not sure of it; I am not a grain sipeoulator.
Suppose you were a grain holder and the maximum price was $2.40, would you hold?

I am not a grain holder,
I am a consumer but that was my understanding of the item as I read it. It was not held -up to the farmer that he was going to get $2.40 a bushel but it was held up that he was not going to get any more than that.

That was the idea I
took from it.
The minister -might answer that question.
