Is it in the power of the supervisor to fix a price for the other grades of grain? This quotation seems to be for No. 1 Northern. As a rule the price for 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, and the other grades are regulated by the law of supply and demand. There being a fixed price for No. 1 Northern, would the intention be to allow all the other grades to be regulated by the demand made for them, or would the Grain Supervisors set the price for each different grade of grain? I am not at all clear upon the point, and I think it would be of valrw to us if we had some information in regard to it.

The Board of Grain Supervisors has complete power to fix the price of grain, and that means not only No. 1 Northern or No. 2, but all grades. No one knows better than my hon. friend that you must have some basis upon which to make a contract, and my own impression is that all grades are valuable and necessary, to the last grade of the grain, and that the prices of the several grades, if fixed by the Board of Grain Supervisors, will be fixed in accordance with the relation of the

grades to one another in point of milling values.
The Order in Council fixing the powers of the Board of Grain Supervisors has been placed on the table of the House, and is available for members of the committee.

Certain powers are defined in the order in council, but very frequently those of us who are not familiar with legal construction may be the better of an explanation as to just exactly what the order in council means, and we would like particularly to have a statement from the minister as to the line in which the Government propose to direct the efforts and activities of this grain commission and what the object to be achieved is.

After all, it seems to me that when, in any important question of this kind, you constitute and empower a body to deal with it the less interference with that body by Government the better; otherwise we should be exposed to the criticism that, whilst appearing to have this thing done by a more or less independent body clothed with power, the Government was simply using this body as an instrument to do what the Government thought best to be done. That is onb side of the question, and my hon. friend will see it is an important side, and that therefore it is necessary to be careful in the selection of the men to whom you trust these great powers. The other side of the question is whether, in any case, the approval of the Government is necessary before the decis-

ions of the Board become effective. I do not carry in my mind just what the powers of the Board aTe as defined in the order in council, but I am quite sure the intention was, after having selected this body of men, to put the power in their hands to the utmost possible extent, so that they, having the matter in -hand an-d being versed in all the ins and outs of this very complex business, might not be interfered with by the Government, or -by politics or parties. At the same time, in reference to regulations of certain kinds, the Government has power of approval.

In regard to certain negotiations that were in progress, I think last fall, in reference to the crop that is now on the market, I understand my hon. friend was negotiating with certain representatives of western grain interests in regard to fixing a price at that time. My understanding was that there was a price offered and a price demanded, and that if the arrangement had been closed at that time those who to some extent represented the farming interests would have accepted a basic price of $1.70 for No. 1 Northern, as against $1.30 offered on behalf of the Government through the Minister of Trade and Commerce. What is the fact in regard to that matter?

I think the facts can be very simply stated. The Canadian Government have been anxious, since the beginning of the war, that Canada should have all possible opportunity of -supplying the demands of Great Britain and the Allies for -such things as Canada produces. We have always been in touch with the British Government and its. different departments in regard to all kinds- of supplies that are required and that can be produced in Canada. We are kept up to the mark in that respect by the people in Canada who have these things to -sell and who are anxious to dispose of them. In carrying out that line of communication, which had never been interrupted from- the time the war began, the question was mooted as to the crop of 1916-17. The British Government were asked whether they had any proposals to -make with reference to the securing of that crop. Different communications took place. I was in London for a little while; I met the Export Wheat Buying Commission there, and talked the matter over with them. The result was that they made an offer for the whole crop surplus for 1916-17, the offer Tunning at about $1.20 or $1.22 a bushel at Fort William. Ultimatelj1' they raised the offer to about
$1.30 or $1.32. I simply did what I thought was my duty; I passed that offer on to persons who appeared to be representative farmers who could take hold of and decide upon any such offer-the Council of Agriculture of the West. I asked these gentlemen to come down and s-ee me. They came, and I told them frankly and -fully what had taken place. They discussed the question with me, went back, and then decided that the terms were not high enough. Consequently, the thing fell through.
Did they make an offer?

If my memory serves me correctly, the price ranged between $1.50, minimum price, and $1.75, maximum price. There again the question of minimum and maximum came up. There is a good deal in favour of the contention that if a maximum price is mentioned and the necessity for the grain is pressing, the grain brings the maximum price.
I believe that one of the gentlemen who was concerned in these negotiations was Mr. Maharg, president of the Council of Agriculture?
Yes.
Has the minister seen Mr. Maharg's statement in regard to these negotiations? If so, does he agree with that statement?

I have seen the interview which was given by Mr. Maharg, but I do not carry it in my memory. In so far, however, as Mr. Maharg's statement is not on all fours with the statement that I have made here, it must come from some misapprehension-not wilful misapprehension-on his part. I think that the attempt was 'made to represent me as pressing the western farmers to take the $1.30 a bushel. Whatever my private opinion was, it was not part of my duty to -press upon them a price which they did not wish to take. I may say frankly that as things looked at that time, it might have been that I thought they should very carefully consider a price at or around those figures. Matters, of course, have greatly changed since -that time.

The farmers who wished to sell last fall did get about $1.75. It will be observed that there is a very wide margin between the $1.75 which the farmers asked last fall for a part of the crop now in the elevators, and the maximum figure of $2.40 that has been fixed by the Board of Grain Supervisors for the remainder of that same crop. I am bringing these facts out

for the purpose of showing that it was not the exorbitant demands of the farmers that made the price $2.40, if that is the price, because certain representative farmers- who, however, did not officially represent the farming community-did, as a matter of fact, believing that that they were acting on behalf of the farmers, offer the crop at $1.75.	,

My hon. friend must bear in mind that conditions change. If there had been no submarine menace, and if many things that happened had not happened, perhaps $1.30 or $1.40 would have been a princely price. As it is, it turned out the other way.

I do not wish to be understood as finding fault with what has been done. But the idea has prevailed in some quarters that the western farmer is taking undue advantage of the situation and is responsible for the high cost of the greatest necessary of life. I merely wish to justify him to this extent: that he did offer to sell out last fall at $1.75, which as a matter of fact, was the maximum price that the large majority of the farmers got.

I do not know what authority Mr. Maharg would have in the West to speak for the farmers of the West. Neither Mr. Maharg nor any other man or association has any right or power whatever to speak for the farmers of the West, Each farmer is master of his own gjrain and can sell it at any price that he can get for it at any time. If the farmer was holding the grain, he was holding it expecting to get a better price, without any regard to any bargain made by Mr. Maharg or anyone else. I do not think too much stress tshould be laid on the fact that some association in the West mentioned a certain figure that might be accepted by the farmers of the West for their product. Such offer was made without authority, and would not be binding upon the farmers. Probably if it had been accepted, no action would have followed.

I do not represent the grain growers or the grain speculators; I represent a very large body of the people who have to eat bread. We are passing a large amount of money into the jhands of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the purpose of dealing with matters affecting grain in the West. As far as I am concerned, that money is voted for some useful purpose.
I am somewhat disappointed at the quantity of information we have been able to obtain

from the minister this afternoon on the question of grain handling and grain prices in the West. Some years ago, long before the war and since this ministry came into office, I took the responsibility, and more or less risk, to mention to the present Minister of Trade and Commerce that his department ought to be in possession of some information in respect to the price of grain from the time it was cut in the field until it got to the elevator and possibly to the mill. On that occasion, the minister answered me with a great deal of witticism and facetiousness and the know-it-all policy that he usually brings forward in matters of this kind, so that any one who doubts him or who looks for information is simply wasting time and beating against a rock from which he gets no result. That seems to be the policy of the minister about these matters. For many months since the war began, we were told by the minister that it was out of the question for the Government to do anything towards regulating those matters, but we kept at them until at last they seemed to change their minds and to think that something could he done, because they started appointing a commissioner, and then they appointed a commissioner to examine the report of the commissioner, and another commissioner to exa-. [DOT]mine the Board of Commissioners. The thing seems to go on like an endless chain without any termination. It would be unkind, I suppose, to say that the Government is taking this method of putting the thing off and giving it over into the hands of the profiteers, the combines, and the trusts, at the expense of the poor people.
I am not saying that is the purpose, but that is the result. If the question were put up to the minister to say: what did those who are getting this $150,000 cash do during the last year to help the miner or the lumberman in Cape Breton by cheapening the cost of flour, I think the minister would have to say that they did nothing at all, and that the Government did not ask them to do anything. I have in my hand a report made by Mr. O'Connor, an official of the Government, on the high cost of living. What he says in paragraph 2 of his conclusion is along the line that I have just suggested, namely, that the Government could have done something much earlier than they did. In paragraph 2, Mr. O'Connor says:
Individual instances of profiteering occurred during the year 1916. These I have already identified. If they had occurred during the present year, since the provision of the Order in Council under which I am acting in the

making of these investigations, I would consider it my duty to recommend that the facts he laid before the proper Attorney General for his consideration as to their criminality.
That is what an officer of the Government says about profiteering in this country, and this profiteering was going on as much, I presume, in connection with wheat and other things, and the reason the criminals are .going to escape is by the *accident of the date of an order in council. If the minister had the public interest at heart, he would not agree that a mere date in an order in council would permit them to escape, when the Government have the power to change that date back and forth just as they like and to make it go back to the date of the War Measures Act. Would the minister take this to be a good answer from anybody else to say that the order in council bore a certain date and that therefore criminality and profiteering could escape? This report has the approval and sanction of the Government because by them it is printed and by them it is 'laid upon the table of the House and distributed amongst hon. members. I further want to bring to the notice of the Government along this line-* and it is quite in accordance with the officialdom in the West and elsewhere for which we are voting money-that although they profess to be getting money from those big concerns for the carrying on of the war, it is merely farcical to he taking it from them in the way it is done, because the big interests simply pile it on the commodities they are producing. If a proper accountant were to investigate the business done by the great profiteers from whom this money is taken, he would find that not only do they put back on the price every dollar that is taken from them by way of a W.ar Profits Tax, but interest on the money, and everything else they can think of is piled on, and that is finally taken out of the pockets of the poor man. That is what has happened in the case of every article that has been taxed. The Ogilvie mills, and some other mills which might be named-I am notnamingthe Ogilvie mills as being greater sinners than the rest-when they sent the prices on flour up to $16 and $17 a barrel, did so for the purpose of getting back the moneys this Government is taking from them as a War Profits Tax. I simply mention this particular case as an illustration so that the minister may understand what I am speaking about. The Department of Trade and Commerce should have a distinct knowledge of every step about this grain from
the time the seed is put into the ground until the grain is handed over to the miller for grinding, or until the flour is put into the bags or barrels for sale. If we had that knowledge, as we surely may and can have it, we would not be obliged to take the most unfair course of asking hon. members here who represent western farming constituencies what they would call a proper price for wheat. That is not a proper question to put to such a member. It is just as unfair a question as to ask me what would he a fair price for coal at the pit mouth, or on board the steamer, because I might be giving away some secrets in connection with the business of the people whom I represent here. So far as the production of coal is concerned, there is no difficulty for any man who follows the matter to know to a half cent what coal should he produced for. He knows the amount of the royalty; he knows the cost to cut it, to hoist it, to put it on the car and to deliver it on board the steamer. Therefore a proper accountant or statistician who follows the matter will know to a half cent whether a coal owner is charging too much or not. The same thing ought to be true about wheat, and if the country wants to know whether a fair price is being charged for wheat, it is not the proper thing for a member on the Government side of the House, in order to make a political point, to ask a member who represents a farming constituency what is a fair price to charge. The department ought to know what it costs to produce wheat and what the charge for flour ought to be to give the millers a fair profit upon their investment and expenditure. We are past that stage in this war when we can speak about prices being regulated by supply and demand.
Whatever may happen after the war, the prdsent conditions demand that the Government arrange for the people getting flour at a reasonable price, and preventing prices from reaching a level which Mr. O'Connor said in his report might be lawful but was certainly not respectaDle. That is the ground I take. The people I represent in this House are non-produoeTS of foodstuffs, hut they are just as useful in the community, and just as useful in the production of the necessities of war as are the people of any other section of Canada. They should not he made the victims of speculators in this way, and he forced to pay $16 or $17 a barrel for flour. In this great Canada of ours there are millions and millions of bushels of grain every year that

we cannot use. There must be some remedy, and we have nobody to look to for a Temedy but the Government and the department. I sincerely trust that some action will soon be taken, without waiting for a new report and then getting some one else to report on the reporter, keeping the question up interminably, with no relief for the people.

My hon. friend seems to
have lost sight of the difficulty that would ensue in a country like this if prices were to be fixed. We live alongside a country with 3,000 miles of frontier, the border, geographically speaking, being an invisible line. Conditions change very rapidly, and I have no doubt that one of the reasons why the board of supervisors were appointed was because of the entry of the United States into this war, and of the two countries having much in common. I have not heard any hon. gentleman express the opinion that it is the duty of this Government to fix a price at which the farmer shall be compelled to sell his grain; I do not think it is the duty of the Government to do that. I think it was fortunate that no action was taken last fall, when it was proposed to fix a price for the farmers' wheat. As events have turned out, they have been to the farmers' advantage. I do not think the people of this country object to the farmer getting the best (possible price for his commodities, but what they do object to is the profit that goes to the middleman between the farmer and the consumer. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has pointed out that the board of supervisors have the power to fix a maximum price for grain. I do not see what good could come of fixing a maximum price unless some organization .backed up by Government buys the grain from, the farmer at that maximum price. On the other hand, I certainly think it would be an advantage to the farmer to have a minimum price fixed, spread over a period of two or three years. But a maximum price is of no advantage unless arrangements are made for buying the grain from the farmer at that price. If such an arrangement were not made, the law of supply and demand would determine the price the farmer would receive. I think the greatest encouragement possible would be given our farmers if we adopted the policy of the British Government of fixing a minimum price spread over a period of two or three years. The farmer who responds to the appeal for greater production necessarily goes to a large expenditure in breaking up more land, (Mr. McKenzie.]
acquiring more machinery, and engaging extra help, and it would be a great encouragement to him to know that he would receive a minimum price, ensuring adequate profit, for his product.

My hon. friend from Cape Breton has intervened with an extraneous subject, remotely connected with what we are discussing, and I shall have to leave him on Hansard in order to get my answer in to the previous questioner before .six o'clock. The order in council reads:
The Board shall make such Inquiries and investigations as from time to time it deems necessary to ascertain what supplies of grain are noV available or will be available. The Board shall ascertain the location and ownership of such grain and what transportation and elevator facilities are available in connection therewith, as well as all conditions connected with the marketing and market price of the same.
The board are given the powers of a commissioner under the Inquiries Act for the purpose of any inquiries they may make. Section 4 says:
The Board shall have power from time to time to fix the price at which grain stored in any elevator may he purchased and the conditions as to price, destination or otherwise under which grain may be removed from such elevator, and may also prescribe what grain shall be sold to millers or milling firms in Canada or elsewhere, and what grain shall be sent to the United Kingdom and the Allied powers.
It will be the duty of the Board to issue such orders and take such action as it deems necessary to facilitate at all times the transportation and delivery of grain in excess of domestic requirements to the United. Kingdom and the Allied powers.
(a)	Any price so fixed shall be subject to the approval of the Chairman of the Board.

Once the board is appointed they are vested with a certain power. Are they expected to exercise that power from the date of their investiture, or do they allow it to lie dormant until an occasion arises that calls for its exercise?
They exercise it whenever they deem necessary.
There may be no exercise of that power?
Quite so.
And they may exercise it on occasion?

Tes, my hon. friend will see that they do not go farther than the storage places. The grain trade goes on as it may, between the time it leaves

the producer and the time it is stored in the elevator.

Is it the intention of the 'Government to establish a relativity of prices, or do they intend to grapple with those cases where industrial disease, blight or something of that description, has made it necessary that some remedy be adopted? Or do they propose to take some scientific plan and establish as I say the relativity of prices and maintain them in order that there may not be this continual unrest and the pulling of one against the other to such an extent that it distorts the whole body of industry?

Does my hon. friend expect me to answer that question offhand, and without hesitation? I think I shall have to ask the privilege of seeing the question in print before I can make an answer that would do justice to myself or to my hon. friend. My hon. friend quite understands it is a most serious undertaking to arrange prices throughout the length and breadth of a country like this, in such a way that everything will flow absolutely smoothly.

In view of the importance of the subject, I think it would be well if the minister would read the whole of the order in council.
Sir GEORGE FOSTER. I have given the gist of the order. In so far as the fixing of prices is concerned the board has the decision as to what is necessary and when it is necessary.

I am sure it would be very valuable information, and much benefit would be derived from the reading of the order in council. Questions might then arise which do not now suggest themselves. For instance, I think the question I asked has brought out a fact which is not covered absolutely in the order in council.

The main provisions of the order in council are:
5.	The Board shall have power to receive offers for the purchase of grain from millers and from the Wheat Export Company, Limited, or from any other person or body representing or acting for the Government of the United Kingdom or for any of the Allied nations or for any combination of the same, and from time to time to fix the prices at which such grain shall be sold.
6.	The Board shall have power to take possession of and sell and deliver to millers or to overseas purchasers at the prices so fixed grain stored in any elevator, and to account and pay over to the orders thereof the proceeds of such sales after deducting all expenses connected with the taking possession, sale and delivery.
7.	The Board shall, as far as possible, and having regard to position and the cost of transportation fix a uniform price throughout Canada for grain of the same kind, quality and grade.
S. Notwithstanding anything in the Grain Act or in the Railway Act, the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada shall have power to order any railway company to provide cars and other transportation facilities for handling grain and to transport as direoted, grain taken possession of or owned by the Board.
9 Every person shall truthfully and promptly answer any inquiry made by the Board or by any person duly authorized on its behalf about any matter within its powers or duties, whether such inquiry is made verbally, in writing, by telegraph, or in any other way.

(b)	To authorize the engaging of clerks, employees, and assistants and the paying of their salaries.
(c)	Creating offences and'providing penalties in respect of violations of any order made by the Board or of any regulation made hereunder.

I am afraid we will have to ask the minister for information as to the policy of the Government in regard to this matter. It might be as well to let it stand until after recess.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock, Mr. Blain in the Chair.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce was reading and explaining the order in council under which the board of grain supervisors was appointed. I would be glad if he would be good enough ito conclude the reading.
I completed it just at six o'clock.

The order in council has conferred upon the board of grain supervisors very remarkable powers. I fancy it would be safe to say that all the power that

was delegated to the Government by Parliament in the War Measures Act has again been delegated by the Government to the board of grain supervisors in the matter of handling and dealing with the grain crop.
As far as defined there.
Does it only apply to wheat; does it apply to other grain?
To grain.
All grain?
Yes.
And to eastern Canada as well 'as western Canada, or only to western Canada?
It applies to all Canada.

It is a matter of very grave interest to every one as to the times and occasions and circumstances under which the board will exercise these very great powers. My hon. friend informed the House that the granting of the powers did not necessarily mean the exercise of the powers, that they would be exercised as occasion demanded.
There is a purpose to be accomplished. If they accomplish that purpose without fixing the price they need not exercise the power.

It is of very great interest to the public to have knowledge as to the circumstances and character of the occasions under which this board will exercise those extraordinary powers. That must be, I presume, a matter of explaining the arrangements or instructions as between the Government and the board. Just on that point I am sure the House and the country will be glad to hear from the minister.

There are no instructions given by the Government, or by any member of the Government, to the board. There are the powers and they exercise the powers in the way in which we have discussed this afternoon. If the board wish to consult with me as the minister under whom they act to a certain extent-that is, they report to me-they have the right of consultation, but I do not consider, and it is not within the four corners of the order in council, that they are to be directed by the Government. Certainly no direction has taken place up to this present time.

The authority vested in this board is an authority to commandeer the grain crop of Canada. The minister, surely, was not a party to placing that enormous, that stupendous, power in the hands of otherwise private individuals without having an appreciation of, or an understanding as to, the circumstances under which such a stupendous power would be exercised. Surely the minister can enlighten us on that point?

Again, I am unable after dinner, as I was before dinner, to give my hon. friend the information which I do not possess, and which, if I gave it to him, I would have to manufacture. I can only answer as to the facts as they are and these aTe the facts: This power is not a power over everything under heaven and on earth. It has to do with a certain line of action to bring about a certain result. The purpose is that the Allies shall get the surplus grain that they want from Canada, -this board is for the purpose of carrying out that idea, and it was given these powers in order that that might be done, going no farther than the storage place, as was explained' before the dinner hour. When the grain is stored then they have a choice of the various powers which I outlined. But the whole purpose of it is that for reasonable and fair prices paid the surplus grain may be put in the hands of the Allies for their purposes, conserving what is necessary for the use of our millers and for Canadian consumption.
Mr. OLIVEfe: Are we to understand that this action on their part does not require confirmation by the Government, no matter what the action may be?
Of course, the Government always have the power, when originating and passing an order in council, to cancel it.

I have pressed the minister very strongly in regard to this matter, and I have done so because of its importance. Although, under this power, the grain supervisors have not control of everything in the heavens above or on the earth beneath, they have control of such an important part of what is on the face of the earth that there is no man in Canada but must feel a very deep interest in the exercise of the tremendous authority vested in them. I do not wish to be understood as finding fault at this stage of the proceedings with the object in view as stated by the minister; that is to ensure that the

grain of Canada shall reach the Allies at reasonable prices. Under the present circumstances of success that is a very proper purpose and is the object of governmental action. But I cannot agree that it is an entirely satisfactory position in -which the people of Canada find themselves under the order in council and subject to the policy as laid down by the minister. I gather from what he said that the board of grain supervisors may commander any amount of grain they please, at any time they please and at any price they please, and that the only remedy the Government has is to cancel their powers, and that the only remedy Parliament would have would be to upset the Government if circumstances would permit of such a thing being done.
I hope to be excused if I say that I do not agree that that is a satisfactory arrangement. This Parliament is, or ought to be, responsible to the peopie of Canada. When one begins to speak about fixing the price of food in order to get plenty of food and more food for the world to live upon, one has to take this into consideration as a primary factor: What reasonable price is it which, while being just and fair to the consumer, will so act upon the producer as to make him feel that he is getting a reasonable return for what he raises, so that he will be impelled to keep on raising and, if possible, to facilitate and increase his production? If you place the fixed value of the product below what meets that reasonable desire, then, of course, you are face to face with an indisposition on the part of the producer to put capital, money, labour and trouble into the raising of the article, and you will perhaps turn him into some other line of production altogether. But what did we do in connection with these elevators? We have a system of allowances and of dockages. The elevator takes in its grain and is allowed on the different kinds of grain, and on the different grades of grain of the same kind, its proper dockages. That is to clean the grain according to the direction, or to the .satisfaction, of the supervisor o,r inspector, and is to clean to grade where the dockage is allowed for cleaning to grade. These elevators, therefore, have a source of surplus. They get, for instance, one and a half per cent on wheat carrying a dockage of five per cent or more. That is pretty dirty wheat and requires a great deal of cleaning. They get an old time allowance which has been running ever since the grain (business was a business in the West. It has no legal status, and never had, but it is a custom grown up, sanctioned and agreed to as between the farmers and the elevator companies. The companies get 30 pounds .per car of wheat, 28 pounds per car of flax, 50 pounds per car of oats and 50 pounds per oar of barley. Up to within two years ago the allowance they received from that old custom was just twice those amounts. Two years ago, or thereabouts, the board of grain oohi-missiomers cut that allowance in two and so diminished to that extent the contribution by the old custom. Then, the elevators may or may not take in certain grades o.f grain; for instance, no grade grain -that is tough or damp, or wheat that is 
not in a condition for warehousing. They are not required to receive that grain. They take it in under contract with the shipper himself and the amount which they take as dockage upon that, or shrinkage, is one per cent of the gross amount. That is, there is a dockage set by the inspector to clean to required grade when it is under five per cent. I read a little while ago the allowances for cleaning up to five per cent and over, these being the amounts of dockage on all clean-to-clean grain or oars where the grain has to be cleaned, re-cleaned and re-cleaned again if necessary until it comes up to the required condition and to the satisfaction of the inspector. Then the elevator takes its dockage and its screenings therefrom and these are the legitimate bases for the overages or surpluses which, they have!
It may Ipe a question as to whether or not the allowances .and dockages have been in the past too great or are too great at the present time. That matter has been very carefully considered by the Board of Grain Commissioners. Uip to the time that we built our own terminal we had nothing to go upon. There .was no comparison as between, for instance, a Government run terminal and a corporate or privately run elevator. The inspection which could possibly be given could not afford ground for a reasonable judgment without our being guided by the running, under Government supervision, of a terminal and our knowing the whole of the .management and inside work of that operation and how it turned out. That way you get your basis for comparison as between that and other elevators, and also as to what is a reasonable return in the way of dockage. Ever since these elevators have been running these overages have, with these dockages and allowances, lessened from time to time. These elevators have been receiving and claiming these surpluses. When the board of grain commissioners took over the work of operating they had an opportunity, amongst other things, of testing out the system for a series of years and coming to conclusions from the real working of the Government elevators as to their overages and their reasonableness. Some two years ago the question came up in an acute form and we were looking into the matter in the department. I laid the question before the Minister of Justice and asked him for his opinion as to whether we had the right to take these overages. After a careful examination of the question the opinion of-the Justice Department was that whoever else had a right

to them the Government had no right, that they were the property either of the elevators or they belonged to the producers of the grain out of whose product these overages were won. There were no possible means of restoring these to the producers of the grain themselves. Therefore, there is only one of two things to do. You can reduce the dockages from year to year so as to bring the overages down to a minimum, or reasonable allowance; or you can, by legislation, affirm that the Government is to take all of these overages, or such portion of them as you may think it reasonable to take, taking all the expenses into account. Inat matter is now, and has been for some time, occupying the attention of the Board of Grain Commissioners and of the department and myself. Before the House rises I propose to bring legislation before Parliament which will in a legal way define to whom these overages shall go. That is a review, though somewhat inadequate, of the question as it comes before the department.

There may be something in what my hon. friend says as to that, but as to whether the screenings, which are taken out of their dockages, go to make up part of the overages, I do not know.

There is no question at all that the 600,000 bushels overage is over and above the screenings, because when a car is inspected, and the inspector marks on it "4 per cent dockage" it means the net weight of that car is four per cent less than the gross -weight, and they are supposed to clean that four per cent out, to bring the weight up to the grade that it is given by the inspector, so that the screenings do not come in, in connection with this amount of overage. All the different scales of dockage that the minister gave us a few minutes ago are supposed to be necessary to make an average car of grain weigh out what is paid for it, and it generally takes something about that to keep the accounts fairly evenly balanced. But when these elevators have 600,000 bushels over and above all that, to my mind there is something very wrong, and remember this is not wheat that is being brought in load by load. This is all carload stuff, all terminal elevator stuff, and it is all carload weights, and there must be something very careless in the manner of weighing in and weighing out, when we find suc-h a tremendous overage as we- have here. It appears that these private elevators have far greater overages than the Government elevators. I understand the weighers are all appointed -by the Government and all Government officials, and have to account to the board of grain commissioners for the work they do. It seems rather strange to me that the private elevators should have so much overage, and the Government elevators should have such a shortage. When

I will certainly
look into the matter and have my officers consider the suggestions made. When my hon. friend was%,speaking about the shortages and overages, he seemed to imply that the Government elevators also, had shortages-
Not all.

-and that the
other elevators had overages. He will see that the terminal elevator at Fort William had fairly large overages as well. The work of some of the internal elevators during their first season was probably not as good nor as accurate as it would be after they got

well started at work. We axe hoping to show a different record for the terminal elevators this year from what they showed the year before.

Perhaps I was wrong
in even suggesting that there might be any intentional crooked work, and I do not wish to make that suggestion, because in the quantity of grain handled, the elevator companies, by being excessively careful to make themselves right, might easily gather up that quantity, as it is only a little over a bushel or a bushel and a half per car, but that is much more than is necessary. The idea that my right hon. friend expressed a little while ago, that one way was to cut down the quantity of dockage the elevators were allowed to take, might perhaps bring about a remedy. I am not so much worried about the overages as over the shortages from which the farmers have to suffer, and for which they do not receive payment.

My hon. friend has to keep this in view-in 1915-16, there were received at Fort William and Port Arthur 286,000,000 bushels of wheat alone. This all commenced away back on the farms of the farmers. It has to go through many vicissitudes, changes, handlings, which cannot be made mathematically accurate. In the first place, there is the interior elevator at the station. The quantity of grain is weighed into that elevator. The first element that comes in is the weighing machine of the elevator into which the farmer loads his grain. It is impossible to make constant and repeated inspections of all these interior elevator weighing equipments. Large weights are necessary, and it would take an army of men to have those examined every now and then during the prevalence of the season. You may to-day send your men there, and they may test that weighing machine and put it into the best of order, and five days later something may have gone wrong and the weighing may not be as accurate as it should be. There is the first contingency in the thousands and thousands of country elevators- where the farmer's grain is weighed. Then when the farmer's grain takes its next excursion, it goes into a car and is carried for thousands of miles down to the terminal elevator. Cars are different one from another; some are new and some are old. There will be leakages and dispersals in that way. But when you come to examine the number of cars that make the journeys and the small number of instances 
in which these deficiencies occur and, therefore, these grievances arise, the latter number is only a small percentage of the whole. The railway company is liable for the quantity of grain that it receives being delivered at the1 terminal elevator. The elevator takes charge of the grain from the car and cannot be debited with more than the car turns out into it, but you come thefe against another fallible piece of machinery, namely, the weighing apparatus. The terminal elevators are under the close supervision of the weighmaster, and the weighmaster at the head of the lakes is a most capable man. If my hon. friend knows him, he will bear me out in that appreciation of Mr. White, who has had charge of the elevators at the head of the lakes for the last three years. The weighing there has been very much improved, and it is as carefully watched and supervised as it is possible for human care to supervise- it. Mistakes will always be made there will be errors and, in some Instances, there may be intentional errors. That is part of a system which you can probably never entirely eliminate, but which by good supervision and constant care you may reduce to a minimum. Therefore, when we speak about those cases that did occur, we must, in the first place, take them in connection with the very large number of cars and the great quantity of grain which is in passage, and we' must also take into account the human element and the mechanical element which come in, either of which is apt to go astray and awry at different times. Taking all these into consideration, I think I am perfectly right in saying that during the last five or six years there has been a very great improvement in the management of the grain handling apparatus under the supervision of -the Grain Board. Whilst there are those individual and sparse cases of trouble and difficulty, in the main, the grain producers and handlers in the West appreciate the system and give it as their opinion that, taken altogether, it is constantly improving, and is, taking human and mechanical fallibility into account, pretty nearly as perfect as it can be made. By increased care and supervision improvement is continually being made, and I hope we shall do something with this matter of overages and shortages that will be satisfactory. The last few years have been a testing and weighing out time. We have now a record which 1 think we can bank upon as being fairly correct, and it is a basis on which legislation may be had and adjustments be made.

I appreciate the fact that oh a percentage basis the elevator companies are, perhaps, not very careless in *having an overage of 612,000 bushels of grain for the year 1916, hut that is not the point I wish to bring before the minister. My point is this: The terminal elevator is an institution that is put there for a certain specified purpose, namely, to handle the grain of the dealer at the point of embarkation.
The point I wish the minister to adjust is this: That .any surpluses there might be over, should not become the property of the terminal elevator company, because it is not legally theiir money. They charge *what is supposed to be a reasonable fee for handling the grain, and there is no more reason why they should be permitted to retain what does not legally belong to them than why the banks should retain unclaimed balances; the two things are in exactly the same position. Surely it is possible to amend the Grain Act in such .a way that the private elevator companies will not be allowed to take groin that does not belong to them.

I quite agree
with my hon. friend, but just how far we can go I cannot say at the moment.

The minister has been willing to give us plenty of information tonight on matters that have come, before the committee, and I should like him to make a statement on the appointment of the new chairman of the grain commission. The farmers of western Canada feel the loss of Dr. Magill very keenly. They looked on him as a real friend on a very important commission, dealing with their affairs and I think many of them felt that the Government would have been warranted in offering him considerable inducements to remain at the head of that commission. I question whether there is any man who understands the grain trade better thorn Dr. Magill. When he was first appointed he was even then an authority, and I am sorry that in appointing his successor the Government did not look around for .another authority. I cannot understand why a Montreal lawyer was chosen as chairman of the grain commission, and I would ask the minister to inform the House of the knowledge this gentleman has of the grain trade-which I am afraid is very little. If the minister had asked me-of course, I know he would not-I think I could have named a very good man in case Dr. Magill could not have been prevailed upon to remain as chairman, and the man I have in
mind happens to he a .political friend of the minister. I have come in touch with the chairman of the Georgian Bay commission within the last year ot two, .and I must confess that he has a very wide knowledge of the requirements of the farmers of western Canada. Mr. Sanford Evans has visited the West .and given addresses there, and he has in my judgment proved himself to. he an .authority on western needs in connection with the grain trade. Mr. Boyd may be a very estimable 'and a very able gentleman, but the people of the West cannot understand why a lawyer from Montreal, who. I am satisfied has no acquaintance with the grain business, should have been appointed to succeed Dr. Magill. Dr. Magill, as I have said, was an authority, and an authority should have been chosen to succeed him, and from all I can gather the gentleman who has been appointed is not an authority by any means. I am sure the minister will give us some reason for the appointment of Mr. Boyd as chairman of that commission.

I shall be very glad to give an explanation, but I cannot guarantee that it will satisfy my hon. friend. There was a time in Dr. Magill's life when he did not understand anything about the grain business. He was a professor in a university, a student above all else, and a man of great mental power and ability. He learned the grain business from that standpoint, a business which was absolutely different from all his training and work up to that time. I merely mention that to show that it is not necessary for a man to have been brought up on a farm, or in a grain exchange or to have been otherwise closely connected with the work of handling and raising grain in order to make himself thoroughly acquainted with the business of helping to conduct the mechanism of the grading, inspection, and handling of grain. I cordially agree with everything my hon. friend has said with reference to Dr. Magill, and I am strongly of the belief that when the people of the West are as well acquainted with Mr. Boyd as they became with Dr. Magill, they will come to look upon him as their friend, and a fair and able administrator of the office of chairman. I used a great deal of care when looking around for some one to take the place of Dr. Magill. I would have kept him if it had been possible to do so, but it was not possible; he had to go and I could not retain him. So I did the best I could to get some one to take his place. Finally Mr. Boyd was selected. Mr. Boyd, I was

informed by gentlemen who are well qualified to judge-and my inquiry was very thorough-is a gentleman of excellent ability, of the very highest character, and thoroughly reliable in every respect. He is, besides, of an energetic, industrious, and studious disposition. He does not take the office simply for the sake of getting the salary attached to the position. After a good deal of correspondence with me he accepted the position with a desire and a liking on his part to make a thorough study of the whole subject, with the object of making himself an approved authority on it. With that ability, that training, and industry and desire of his, I am quite certain he will prove a success as chairman of the commission. He is associated with practical men who understand the grain business, both from the elevator and the farmer's point of view, and consequently the commission is broad in that it can call upon men of different kinds" of experience and ability.
There is one thing to the advantage of Mr. Boyd, and that is, he has had a legal training and is in good standing as a lawyer. To my mind, a legal knowledge and legal training plays a very important part in the successful carrying out of the duties of chairman of the grain commission. These are the reasons why I chose Mr. Boyd. He has undertaken the work, and I bespeak for him a fair trial. I shall be very much disappointed indeed if he does not turn out to be a very successful member and chairman of the commission.

I think I was right in stating that Dr. Magill was an authority before he became chairman of the grain commission. While he was connected with Dalhousie University, the Saskatchewan Government appointed him chairman of a commission 'to inquire into the elevator question, and he there acquired a considerable knowledge of the grain business.
He had the knowledge and the qualifications to become chairman of the grain commission. He was also thoroughly acquainted with the grain trade of the West. The gentleman who has been appointed to succeed him may be all the minister says he is, but he has not the knowledge of the grain business. I hope he acquires it as rapidly as the minister thinks he will, and I hope he may be a success.

I agree entirely
with what has been said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce with regard to Mr. Leslie Boyd. Admitting that a political fSir George Foster.]
friend of the Government had to be named, I think the Government could not have chosen a better man for the position. As the minister says, Mr. Boyd is a good lawyer and a practical, man in every respect, and he was a good alderman of the city of Montreal for many years, which is something.

It certainly is
something.

He resigned his
seat to take up this new position, and I think the Government has made a first-class appointment. I believe my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mjr. Buchanan) 'knows Mr. Boyd.

I met him with my
hon. friend (Mr. L. A. Lapointe)

The only thing
that seems to worry my hon. friend from Lethbridge is the fact that Mr. Boyd may not have very much knowledge of the grain business. That may foe so, but I am sure he will acquire that knowledge as quickly as he acquired other knowledge which was useful to him. I feel he will be a practical man, and a splendid man for the position.

I would like to ask the
minister in regard to the permission given to the railway companies last winter to refuse the carriage of grain from points in Alberta to Fort William. During a part of last winter the railway companies operating in Alberta refused to carry grain to Fort William. Although they would take it to the internal elevators. I would like to know under what conditions that refusal was made?

Under conditions of great congestion and insufficient haulage which obtained there for a considerable time. A great quantity of the grain was insufficiently stored and there was great necessity of getting it moved as quickly as possible. It was entirely a matter of railway transport, and I consulted with the chairman of the railway board, Sir Henry Drayton, and he took the question up with the railway companies, and instituted this system of more rapid transit of the grain from the places where it was originally stored, and where in very many cases it was insecurely stored. A certain railway division was told to use its cars to bfing the grain to a transition point, and then go back and get more, using the cars as quickly as possible, in order to take away the great quantities of wheat which were lying there
10 p.m. and about the removal of which the people were rightly clamour-

ing. Then another railway took the grain at an internal elevator, say Saskatoon, and moved it the other distance down. If the cars which were loaded at the distant points west of Saskatoon had to go all the way to Fort William and back, there was a usage and a delay of cars. If they could use their somewhat insufficient force to go short distances and do rapid haulage, they got the advantage of storage in a safe place, with as good conditions in the matter of cost as could possibly be given. The two sets of cars working together constituted a more expeditious way than could be got by any other means of handling the grain and of relieving the congestion in country places. This system was worked out by the chairman of the Railway Board, and the railway companies. Everything possible was done with the idea of moving the grain as quickly as it could be moved from the congested and threatened, districts. I say threatened, because of the insecure storage much of the grain being stored in open fields.
By what authority did the railway companies refuse to take the grain?

If the railway companies refused to take grain, I suppose they refused to take it on the ground that all railway companies refuse at certain times of congestion to add to the congestion by piling more grain into cars which cannot find an ultimate resting place to be unloaded, and the cars get back again. When you have congestion towards the front, and that congestion becomes so great that if you pile more freight in, it simply adds to the difficulty, then as a matter of sensible haulage the railway company says: We cannot take any more until this forward portion is relieved. Last year there was this congestion of freight from New York, Baltimore, Boston, and Portland. The freight was piled up along thousands oE miles, and every storage facility was filled to the very roof. Finally, it became necessary that these embargoes should be put on. The embargo is a part of the system of railway transport, and although it may be unsatisfactory for the person who has a car of grain and wants it taken out at a certain time, in the end it w.orks out for better transportation in general.

I shall have to take issue with my Tight hon. friend on this point. I would like to know, if he can tell me-and if he cannot the Minister of Railways is beside him and may be able to give the information-whether the railway companies refused on their own initiative to haul the
grain, or if they did it under authority from any department of the Government, or any commission acting for the Government?

So far as I know the embargo was on, and I received notice of it. As soon as I was notified, I immediately took the question up to see what could 'be done in order to relieve conditions.
I got in touch with the man who is best able, taking a general view of the matter and having general authority, to bring order out of confusion and to regulate so that the best haulage might be had. He went into the question very thoroughly with the railway companies, and they did the best they could.
The minister has not mentioned the name of this gentleman.
Sir Henry Drayton.

Was the course followed
by the railway companies taken with the authority of the railway commission?

I am informed
the embargoes are always put on by the railway companies themselves.

If they did it with the
authority of the railway commission, the people who were affected will have to hold the Government directly responsible for the consequences they have suffered.

I do not know
whether that reasoning is correct.

That is the reasoning I
have to make. I wish to put the case to the Government as forcibly as it is possible to put it. There is supposed to be a public right which is expressed in what is known as the Common Carriers law. That is a law, which, as far as I know, was never set at defiance publicly and without cause until last year. All that my right hon. friend has said about the stress of circumstances compelling the railway companies to do thus and so on account of certain conditions existing does not apply, because these conditions did not exist last year. They existed the year before, but not last yeaT. Last year it was not a question of a heavy crop but of a short crop.
It is more than the crop; it has to do with the conditions of general freightage.

Last year there was a very short crop and there was not the same burden of tonnage as there was in previous

years. There was not at any time last winter a shortage of storage at Fort William and if the railways did not haul grain forward to Fort William and to Minneapolis it was because they refused to do it and not because they could not do it. The result was very serious loss and damage to the farmers, particularly of Alberta. These railway companies offered to haul the farmers' grain to the interior storage elevator at Calgary, which would be a back haul, or to Saskatoon or Moosejaw. For what purpose were these storage elevators built? They were supposed to be built for the advantage of the farmers. They were supposed to meet a condition of grain blockade as a result of shortage of storage at the head of the lakes or of undesirable weather conditions. Neither of these conditions prevailed last year. Whether the action taken by the railway companies was simply to make matters easy for themselves, or whether it was taken at the instance of the Government in order to turn their elevators into earning propositions, I do not know, but I do know that the farmer producer of Alberta lost very considerably because of the failure of the railways to take the grain forward to Fort William or Minneapolis when it was desired that it should go forward. The statement that the railway companies were short of cars is a statement that I for one cannot give credence to. The railways were able to handle the crop production of the year before thopgh immensely larger than the crop of last year. Everybody recognizes that if they had difficulties last year' they were able to handle that immense crop of the year before during the period of transportation. Therefore, as there was no destruction of rolling stock in the meantime, as they still had it, there was no reason to believe they were not able to haul that grain forward as the needs of the country demand that they shall carry it forward; that is when the farmer desires to ship it. Any other construction placed upon the duty of the railways to the public is a wrong construction.
It is fitting in this connection, that I should draw to tne attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) the action taken by the railway companies in the vicinity of Edmonton in regard to the haulage of coal, where at the beginning of winter, and at the time the Southern Alberta coal strike was on, the railways, because of some disagreement between themselves, or for some other reason that no man can find out, absolutely tied up

the coal industry between Edmonton and the consumers of coal on the prairies at a most critical time of the year. I am not one of those who look upon the railway companies with any desire to see them do other than prosper but I do want to see it impressed upon them that they enjoy the privileges which they do enjoy as the servants and not the masters of the public. I look to this Government, in the discharge of their responsibilities and duties to see that the railway companies do their duty to the public as they did not do it last year in the province of Alberta.

Not long ago a deputation of Vancouver business men visited Calgary and made the statement that after seeing some members of the Government in Ottawa it would not be long before grain was moving westward to the Pacific. They said they had the assurance of one of the members of the Government that they were going to force the grain to the West and through by the Pacific route. The only member of the Government ;who could make a statement of that kind that would be official would be the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is in charge of the operations of the grain trade and I would like to know if he could give us any information about forcing grain through by the Pacific route.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce never gave an assurance of that kind and never had any thought of that kind. It is not within his power to force grain. Grain has to go according to the natural channels. Under the circumstances which have existed for two years at least, and which especially have existed during the past year, any attempt to force grain through by way of Vancouver and the Panama canal' is absolutely impossible. My hon. friend will see that in a moment if he begins to think over the conditions as they exist. It is desirable that as soon as possible a shipment of grain shall be made by Vancouver and through the Panama canal for various reasons. Such a shipment, as soon as it can be made under anything like normal conditions, will solve two questions which are a little in doubt. One of them, not very much in doubt, is as to whether grain in bulk' will bear the passage through the canal without being injured or going wrong. The other is as to the commercial and economic possibilities of shipping grain through that route. But under these abnormal conditions you can settle that sec-

ond question. I am in communication now *with the British authorities with the view of having one of the British vessels which are being constructed on the Pacific coast, when she is finished and sails for Great Britain, take a cargo of bulk grain for the purpose of settling a doubt that has been expressed, although I do not think there is very much in it, namely, that bulk grain cannot be carried through the Panama canal. I believe there is no doubt it can be carried, and I hope before the season is over that a shipment of bulk grain will in that way go through from the West and through the Panama canal.
Trade and Commerce-.Supervision lake and ocean freight rates, $6,000.

There was a charge
this summer that lake freight rates were very high. Does this vote mean that there is any supervision or that any supervision can be exercised?

This is a vote that was put in the year before last when I contemplated the appointment, if I could get the proper man, of a supervisor of lake and ocean freights. But the conditions have been so abnormal on the ocean and, to a certain extent, upon the lake, that I have not made the appointment, and we will have to get back to something like normal times before any good can come from the appointment of such an officer. So that this is a vote for the appointment of such an officer when the time becomes suitable.
Is this merely a vote for an officer who will secure information, or is it a vote for an officer who will exercise some authority?

Primarily, it is for an officer who will secure information. The Department of Trade and Commerce has a system of subsidized services running to different parts of the world. There is always a question of freight rates coming up. We had no expert in the department, and I had not myself the expert knowledge which is necessary to guide decisions which the department and th$ minister must give oftentimes with reference to freight rates. I wanted an officer of that kind who would be the information bureau of the department with reference to freight rates, and then, with that information, the department could probably do more than it has been doing, even in
the past, in the regulation or control of freight rates.
What measure of control or regulation has the Government in regard to lake rates?

It has none. We have no subsidized services on the lakes, and we only have power to control or regulate the freight rates charged by subsidized services. There has .been, as my hon. friend knows, negotiations with the British Government for some years back with reference to getting a concerted action between the United Kingdom and Canada, and, if possible, the United States, with reference to some general supervision of ocean rates. But nothing has transpired, although a good deal of attention has been given to it, and the war, of course, has stopped all those matters for the time being.
Is Canada still paying subsidies to the mail steamship lines?
Yes.
The Government has not any control of rates?
All the contracts with subsidized lines are signed, of course, by the minister, and the schedule of rates chargeable is within the control of the minister.
For freights?
Yes.
From what I have heard, the minister must be very liberal in the allowance for freights, because the general impression is that freights are very high.
The freights are very high, and fifteen hundred thousand ministers could not have done much during war time to make any different rates.

I would suggest that, when rates are so high, and business demands that they be high, might not the subsidy we pay them be fairly withdrawn, on the same principle that the bonus that we pay to the lead smelting companies, when prices are beyond a certain figure, is reduced? The steamship companies are making more money than before the war, and surely we might save the money we are paying for subsidies.

We might if we took away the subsidies, and we would then have no longer any control over the lines, which are mail lines. These mail lines must conform, in their dates of sailing, and



as to the ports of sailing, and the like of that, to their contract with us. We must have control of those things for the sake of the mails, and we keep that control and exercise it, because we subsidize them. They have to sign contracts and abide by those contracts. We might also impose certain rates of freight on them, but if the rates that we fixed were less than the rates that could be got from ports to the south of us, we would run the risk of losing our lines entirely.

I do not wish to speak
about ocean rates, but in regard to the lake boats, there was a time this season when the boats were charging seven cents >a bushel from Fort William to Midland. That is a very high rate. It was not a case of supply and demand, but a case of hold up. The lakes are common property between C'-mada and the United States, and if it is not possible for this Uovemimenc to control the grain rate on lake (boats on our side of the lakes, perhaps the Government would consider the matter of entering into a reciprocity treaty with the United States, so as to secure a control of rates on the lake lines. This is a matter isurely within our reach, and while I am perfectly willing that the companies should make reasonable profits, everybody will admit that a seven cent rate is not within the hounds of reason, and is not a case of payment for services rendered, but a case of hold up, and should not he permitted.

There might be, in normal times, some chance of a dual control toy co-operation in that way, in regard to the traffic on the lakes, although it is a complex question, taking into account the ore and coal and grain, which constitutes the chief pant of the freight, but at the present time I do not think any thing would come from an attempt to regulate the rates between the two countries. iMy bon. friend does not take that seven cent rate that he spoke about as an index of the general rate. I think the rates were about two or two and a quarter cents the last time I inquired.
Progress reported.

The House in Committee on Rill No. 13, to consolidate 'and amend the Railway Act. -Hon. Frank Cochrane.
Mr. Blain in the Chair.

On the 18th July I
accepted an amendment prepared by my hon. friend from Rouville and proposed by '
[Sir George Foster.!
the hon. gentleman from Rimouski, which reads as follows:
All railway employees on local passenger trains running in the province of Quebec, having to deal with the travelling public, shall he conversant with the English and French languages from and after January 1, 1919.
There has been strong objection to this amendment on the ground that it would cut men out of their seniority. For instance, a man running on a freight train to Prescott or Brockville would be prevented from being promoted, say, to a passenger train running to Montreal, because he was not able to speak French. I feel that the amendment suggested by the member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright) will meet thq situation far better. I move that section 302 be amended by adding thereto the following as subsection 3:
After the 1st day of January, 1919, the Board may from time to time make such orders and regulations as it may deem advisable to provide that all or any railway employee on local passenger trains running in the province of Quebec shall be conversant with the English and French languages.
I am sure that none of us want to injure the railway'men, or deprive them of their right of promotion. Neither my hon. friend nor myself thought of this when the amendment was made. I hope that the committee will accept the proposed change.

I thought that the
amendment had been drafted in such a way as to meet all possible objections. It was at the suggestion of the Minister of Railways and Canals that the amendment was drafted in that form. However, I am sure that nobody would like to cause any injustice to the conductors. My hon. friend realizes that there are some grievances-I mentioned some the other day. I hope that the board of railway commissionefis will not allow this amendment to remain on the statute book as a dead letter. Under the circumstances, I agree to accept my hon. friend's further amendment, because I know that he is well disposed towards the conductors and towards the public. The very fact of inserting the amendment now moved by my hon. friend and the publicity the matter has had since it was brought before the committee may produce the desired effect of inducing the conductors on all local trains in the province of Quebec to learn both languages.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.

Sections 379, 380 and 381 provide for a statistical return to the minister him-

But more than that, being not under one management as regards methods, schedules and information to be gathered, they do not serve the purposes of comparison, and the idea is that these statistics should be gathered by the -central department of statistics, so as to prevent duplication and confusion. This also has the other effect that you do not bother the companies with a duplication or a triplication of demands upon them for practically the same information. My suggestion is that all the statistics are provided for in section 384 and the co-related sections.

Has the minister gone over this copy to see that the provisions of what is section 384 in my copy and which I suppose will be 383 in the minister's copy are provided by the present section 384. Section 384 in my copy or section 383 in the minister's copy says:
All returns made in pursuance of any of the-provisions of this Act last preceding shall be privileged communications, and shall not be evidence in any court whatsoever, except in any prosecution for,-
(a)	default in making such returns in accordance with the requirements of this Act;
(b)	perjury in making any oath required by this Act in connection with such returns;
(c)	forgery of any such return; or,
(d)	signing any such return knowing the; same to be false.

That is an important provision. It is quite right that many of these statistics should be treated as confidential, but if the company makes a false return, or fails to make a proper return, there ought to be some right to sue it for the purpose of securing a conviction. I turn to subsection (5) of the section which the minister purposes retaining, and it seems to carry out the same idea, but I would like to know whether it goes far enough. The subsection says:
The Board may authorize any part of such information to he made public when, and in so far as there may appear to the Board to be good and sufficient reason for so doing.
I suppose that would give the board the power to go into any court of law.

Yes. There is a proviso after that:
Provideid that if the information so proposed to be made public by the Board, is of such [DOT]character that such company would, in the [DOT]opinion of the Board, be likely to object to the publication thereof, the Board shall not authorise such information to be published without notice to such company.

There are no powers taken away. I only want to make plain that there is nothing to prevent the board using this information for the purpose of punishing negligence or the making of false returns.

On the motion of Hon. Mr. Cochrane for the third reading of the Bill.

Might I respectfully urge that the House consent to the third reading to-night, as I understand the Senate have very little before them to-morrow and would be able to devote the whole day to this Bill, if passed.

I understand that some hon. gentlemen who are not now present have some amendments to offer, and I would therefore suggest that the Bill be not given its third reading until the next sitting of the House.
